summary: This informational memo describes ways an internet service provider can add IPv6 to an existing IPv4 network without disrupting IPv4 service. It analyses the scenarios, evaluates how useful the existing transition mechanisms are in each, and points out known challenges.

plainLanguage.summary: An internet provider cannot just switch its network over to IPv6. This memo sets out ways to add IPv6 while the old IPv4 service keeps running, and works through the choices for the backbone, for customer connections and for running the network.

subtitle: How an internet service provider adds IPv6 to a running IPv4 network without disturbing the old service.

tldr.problem: An internet service provider on IPv4 has to add IPv6 service and global address space for its customers, but it cannot replace IPv4 overnight or let the IPv4 service break while it works.
tldr.mechanism: The memo divides the work into four stages of IPv6 readiness and then lists the actions for each part of the network: turning the backbone dual-stack, reaching customers with tunnels before their own gear is upgraded, and updating operations.
tldr.outcome: Providers get a deployment plan matched to their own topology, covering backbone and customer transition, routing, customer configuration, traceability and the security points to settle first.

today: RFC 4029 is an Informational memo published in March 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a deployment guide rather than a specification: it describes how an ISP can add IPv6 to an IPv4 network without interrupting the IPv4 service.

sections.title: Why an ISP Needs a Transition Plan
sections.content:
When an ISP deploys IPv6, the goal is to give its customers IPv6 connectivity and global address space. The new service has to be added on top of an existing IPv4 service, and adding it must not interrupt that IPv4 service.

This memo sets out a small set of scenarios for doing that. It evaluates which of the transition mechanisms that already exist are relevant in each scenario, and points out where they lack essential functionality. The document covers services that include both IPv6 and IPv4; it does not cover IPv6-only service, and it does not describe different access or network technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: An internet provider cannot just switch its network over to IPv6. This memo sets out ways to add IPv6 while the old IPv4 service keeps running.

sections.title: The Parts of an ISP Network
sections.content:
A generic ISP network has two main parts, the backbone and the customer connection networks, plus building blocks such as network and service operations. The backbone is the rest of the infrastructure: the parts of the provider edge equipment that face the core, the core routers, and the border routers used to exchange routing information with other providers. The customer connection is the part a customer uses to connect, and it includes the customer premises equipment, the last hop link, and the parts of the provider edge equipment that interface to that link. Network and service operation hosts the management, supervision, accounting, billing and customer management applications the ISP needs to run.

A network that natively supports both IPv4 and IPv6 is called a dual-stack network. In some cases, for example an incumbent national or regional operator, a customer connection network may have to be shared between different ISPs, which brings extra architectural constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Any ISP network splits into three pieces: the backbone that connects its own sites, the connection that reaches each customer, and the systems that run and bill the network.

sections.title: Four Stages of IPv6 Readiness
sections.content:
The memo divides the transition into stages. A stage is a snapshot of the network in terms of IPv6 maturity, and because the network keeps changing, a stage measures how far along the ISP is. A network segment can only be in one stage at a time, but the whole ISP network can be in different stages, and the move between stages does not have to happen all at once.

There are four likely stages. Stage 1, Launch, is an IPv4-only ISP with an IPv4 customer, which is the natural starting point; the first step is to obtain a prefix allocation, typically a /32, from the appropriate regional registry, and to establish IPv6 connectivity to upstream providers and peers. Stage 2a, Backbone, has a dual-stack backbone and IPv4-only customer connections, so a tunnel carries IPv6 through the IPv4 customer connection. Stage 2b, Customer connection, has an IPv4 backbone and a dual-stack customer connection, so IPv6 traffic is carried by tunneling over the existing IPv4 backbone or in a separate IPv6 overlay network. Stage 3, Complete, has native IPv6 and IPv4 in both the backbone and the customer connection networks.

From Stage 1 the ISP can move in three directions: upgrade the backbone first, upgrade the customer connection network first, or introduce IPv6 in both as needed. Because backbone IPv4 networks evolve anyway, with firmware replacements and new routers, they can be made ready for IPv6 without much extra investment. The document warns that IPv6 features should be requested from vendors for all new equipment from the outset, because removing hardware that cannot do IPv6 later may take significant time and effort.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names four stages of readiness, from an IPv4-only network to a fully dual-stack one. An ISP can move through them in different orders, and different parts of its network can sit at different stages.

sections.title: Backbone Transition Actions
sections.content:
The backbone starts as IPv4-only and ends fully dual-stack, with intermediate steps. The first step uses tunnels or dedicated links and leaves the existing routers unchanged, so only a small set of routers have IPv6 capability. The second step adds dual-stack routers progressively. The final step is reached when all or almost all routers are dual-stack. The memo notes that each intermediate step is possible but none is mandatory, and that an ISP is likely to stay in the early steps for a long time if only a few customers connect.

If MPLS is already deployed, providing IPv6 over it needs either LDP or RSVP-TE to signal IPv6 label switched paths, which might require changes in the MPLS core. The memo lists four approaches: require native IPv6 routing and forwarding in the MPLS network, require native routing and the setting up of IPv6 label switched paths, use only configured tunneling over IPv4 label switched paths, or use the BGP tunneling mechanism for IPv6 over IPv4 or MPLS. The first two are the best targets, though the first may be impossible if the installed equipment cannot do high performance native IPv6 forwarding, and the second may be impossible if the ISP cannot add IPv6 label switched path setup to the MPLS control plane. The BGP tunneling approach can serve as an interim measure; configured tunneling over IPv4 label switched paths is roughly equivalent but may lack scalability in larger networks.

Routing needs its own decisions. The IPv6 interior gateway protocol is either OSPFv3 or IS-IS, and the central choice is whether IPv4 and IPv6 run in separate processes or the same one. Separate processes cost more memory and CPU but keep a fault in IPv6 routing from touching IPv4 routing, which is why they may be preferable early on. Using one process for both is usually preferable operationally. If IS-IS is used for both address families, the IPv4 and IPv6 topologies must be convex unless the multiple-topology extensions are implemented. For the exterior gateway protocol, BGP is used for both internal and external sessions, with multiprotocol extensions allowing IPv6 routing information and BGP sessions over IPv6; separate sessions for each address family are the most common practice. IPv6 routing information should be carried over IPv6 transport, because IPv6 connectivity may work when IPv4 is down, the best route for one address family is not always the best for the other, and the two logical topologies may differ. For multicast, PIM-SM and PIM-SSM work with IPv6, while MSDP, which exchanges information about multicast sources in IPv4, is intentionally not defined for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Upgrading the backbone can be done in steps: first carry IPv6 in tunnels over the old routers, then add dual-stack routers one at a time, and finally make everything dual-stack. The memo also works through the routing choices.

sections.title: Customer Connection Transition Actions
sections.content:
Customer connection networks are built from a small set of provider edge devices and a large set of customer premises equipment, often on different technologies depending on the customer type and bandwidth. IPv6 service can be provided by tunneling, with the tunnel terminating at the customer premises equipment or on another device in the customer's network. Defined tunneling techniques include configured tunnels with a tunnel broker, 6to4 and Teredo. Some are based on an addressing plan independent of the ISP's allocated prefixes, while others use part of the ISP's own prefix, and using the ISP's address space is usually preferable.

Several practical details decide whether a tunnel works. In most cases 6to4 and ISATAP are incompatible with NATs, and UDP encapsulation for configured tunnels has not been specified. Dynamic, non-permanent IPv4 address allocation makes tunneling harder to deploy, especially if no protocol with authentication, such as PPP for IPv6, is used. NAT traversal can be avoided if the NAT forwards protocol 41 and is configured to do so. Firewalls in the path can also break tunnels, and the administrator has to open a hole for them. Terminating the tunnel at the customer premises equipment usually simplifies all of this, provided that device supports the tunneling mechanism or is upgraded to do so. Large end sites usually have a managed network, so dual-stack access service is often possible, although customer premises equipment upgrades may be needed. Teredo is not applicable there, because it can only give one host IPv6 connectivity rather than the whole site, and 6to4 is not recommended because of its reliance on relays and provider-independent address space.

The remaining work covers authentication and access control, which can reuse the IPv4 access control unless the provider wants different results for the two address families, and RADIUS traffic for IPv6 service can be carried over IPv4. Configuring customer equipment is hard, especially remotely, so automatic configuration of the delegated prefix, the DNS server address and possibly an NTP server address is beneficial, using DHCPv6 when user identification is required. The memo also requires traceability, so that a specific IPv6 address or prefix can be tied to a customer, and ingress filtering toward the customers everywhere, using access lists or unicast reverse path forwarding, to ensure traceability, to prevent denial of service with spoofed addresses and to keep the management infrastructure safe.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer side is upgraded with tunnels first, carrying IPv6 across the existing IPv4 network until the customer's own equipment can speak IPv6. The memo lists what usually gets in the way: firewalls, address translation and dynamic addresses.

sections.title: Operations, Follow-On Work and Security
sections.content:
Network and service operation work falls into categories: setting up IPv6 connectivity to upstream providers and peers, configuring IPv6 on network devices, IPv6 network management, IPv6 monitoring, IPv6 customer management, and security for network and service operation. Some of these need a native IPv6 transport and some do not. As a first step, device configuration and network management can run over IPv4, since IPv6 management information bases are available, but some monitoring functions, such as those using ICMPv6 messages, need IPv6 transport. A practical problem on many platforms is the inability to retrieve separate IPv4 and IPv6 traffic statistics from dual-stack interfaces using SNMP.

The memo lists the work that still needs specifications in the IETF. A tunnel server or broker mechanism is needed for the cases where customer connection networks cannot be upgraded, and an IPv6 site multihoming mechanism has to be developed. Two items were already in progress: 6PE for MPLS was identified as a required mechanism, and IS-IS for multiple topologies was noted as helpful in some environments but not strictly required.

On security, the document says it introduces no new security issues and that the security considerations of each mechanism are described in the document that defines it. It adds that IPv6 brings new classes of threat or requires new protocols and operational models, that the more complex the transition mechanisms become the harder they are to manage and analyse, and that simple mechanisms are therefore preferable. It also flags three questions that need explicit consideration when adopting IPv6: how to do access control over shared media or shared customer connection media, how to manage configuration management security in those environments, for example DHCPv6 authentication keying, and how to manage customer traceability if stateless address autoconfiguration is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The operating side of the ISP also has to change: management, monitoring, billing and customer records. The memo finishes with the security points a provider should settle before it starts.
